payload.answer: It depends on which kind of issue, and the distinction is important. If covering a branch shows the branch is UNREACHABLE, deleting it is the fix, not a refactor -- that is the zero-exemptions rule working as intended, and covering it is impossible by definition. If the code is merely awkward -- an overcomplicated conditional that is reachable and correct -- cover the design as it stands and raise the refactor as a separate item. Refactoring under a coverage mandate is how a coverage task quietly becomes an unreviewed redesign, and it makes the diff impossible to review against its stated purpose. The one thing never acceptable is changing production behaviour to make a test easier to write.
